video.title: [Video Tip] Breaking Down the Flavor Elements of Beer and Food

keyPoints.line: opposites make each other stand out.

read.bigIdea: Three ways beer and food work.
read.where: Cicerone’s examples: **complement**, where shared flavors resonate (a clove-spiced curry with a **Dunkelweizen**’s clove); **contrast**, where an opposite makes the other stand out (a **gueuze**’s acidity makes **mussels** taste richer and sweeter); and **cut**, where **carbonation**, **sourness** and **bitterness** lift fat off the palate. More detail: bitterness can turn **metallic** with oily fish; **roast** suits chocolate and char; **salt** makes sweetness seem stronger.
read.mixup: Bitterness doesn’t suit everything: with oily fish it can taste metallic.
read.sayIt: The bubbles in this one will cut right through the richness.

video.title: CraftBeer.com: Pairing Craft Beer and Cheese

read.bigIdea: Match the cheese’s strength with the beer’s.
read.where: The Brewers Association and American Cheese Society: **carbonation**, acidity and bitterness cut through fat, and **malt** complements creamy, nutty, caramel flavors. Match **intensity**: delicate beers with **young** cheese, bold beers with **aged** cheese. Starting points: fresh cheese with **wheat** beers; **blue** cheese with **IPA**; aged **cheddar** with **stout**; **Brie** with golden ales; washed-rind cheeses with **Belgian** ales. Serve cheese at **55–65°F**, mildest to strongest.
read.mixup: Cold cheese from the fridge has little flavor. Let it warm up.
read.sayIt: With the blue cheese, an IPA is a great match.

sections.name: Cooking with beer and beer dinners

read.where: Reducing beer **concentrates** what doesn’t evaporate: **bitterness** climbs and can turn harsh, malt sweetness **caramelizes**, and roast gets more burnt; **hop aroma** and fruity esters fade. So use hoppy beer **uncooked** (an IPA vinaigrette) and malty beer in braises. For **beer dinners**, the Brewers Association suggests a 4–6 oz welcome beer, then **3–4 oz** per course, building **intensity** as the meal goes; past about **10 beers** most palates are tired.
read.mixup: A very hoppy IPA in a long braise turns bitter. Pick a malty beer for the pot.

read.where: The Brewers Association suggests starting with **flavor words** guests know: **crisp, clean, bitter, fruity, tart, roasty**, rather than “IPA” or “stout”. **Ask** what they usually like, then pick. It groups beers into flavor families: **Clean & Crisp**, **Malty & Sweet**, **Fruity & Spicy**, **Sour & Funky**, **Hoppy & Bitter**, **Dark & Roasty**. Cicerone asks for the same precision with food: not just “seared scallop”, but a caramelized, **toffee-like** sear with a sweet center.
read.mixup: Dark doesn’t mean heavy, and hoppy doesn’t mean strong. Describe what’s in the glass.
read.sayIt: Do you like something crisp and clean, or something with more flavor, like fruity or roasty?

video.title: Beer Talk: Certified Cicerone Test Format and How Hard Is It?! - Ep. #1286

read.bigIdea: The next step, if you want it.
read.where: The **Certified Cicerone** exam needs a passed **Certified Beer Server** and legal drinking age. The **written** part (short answer and essay) is taken **online**, three hours, closed book and proctored. The **tasting** (13 samples: off-flavors, style, fitness to sell) and a short **demonstration** are **in person**. You need **80% overall** and at least **70% on tasting**. Cicerone suggests about **six months** of study for an experienced pro, **one to two years** for many.
read.mixup: Our Beer Specialist certificate is the restaurant’s. The Certified Cicerone title only comes from Cicerone’s exam.
